topic: Kodak invented the digital camera and it destroyed them
title: Kodak Invented the Digital Camera. Then It Killed Them
alt_titles: The Invention Kodak Hid in a Drawer
How Kodak Lost Everything to Its Own Invention
pinned_comment: Can you think of a company today that is making the same mistake Kodak made? Let me know.
sources_to_check: Steve Sasson's 1975 prototype: about 8 pounds, 0.01 megapixels, 23 seconds per photo
Kodak's share of US film sales around 90 percent in the 1970s
Peak of about 145,000 employees in the late 1980s
Ofoto sold to Shutterfly in 2012 for about 24 million dollars
Instagram sold to Facebook for 1 billion dollars in 2012
description:
In 1975, a young Kodak engineer built the world's first digital camera. His bosses' reaction? Nice, but don't tell anyone. Thirty-seven years later, Kodak filed for bankruptcy, killed by the technology it had invented.

This is the story of how one of the most powerful brands in history, a company so big that "a Kodak moment" became part of the English language, saw the future before anyone else and still lost.

• George Eastman and the birth of a giant
• The secret business model: film, not cameras
• The 1975 prototype nobody wanted
• Digital cameras, smartphones and Instagram
• The 2012 bankruptcy and the lesson for every company

segments.text: In 1975, a 24 year old engineer walked into a meeting with a strange machine. It was the size of a toaster, it weighed around 8 pounds, and it took 23 seconds to save a single black and white picture onto a cassette tape. It was the first digital camera in history. The company he worked for looked at it, and according to the engineer himself, the reaction was something like: that's cute, but don't tell anyone about it. The company was Kodak.

Thirty seven years later, Kodak filed for bankruptcy. It was not destroyed by a competitor with a better idea. It was destroyed by its own invention, an invention it had kept in a drawer while the rest of the world caught up. To understand how that is even possible, we need to understand how Kodak really made its money. And it was not by selling cameras.

The story starts in the 1880s with a man called George Eastman. Back then, photography was a nightmare. You needed heavy equipment, glass plates, chemicals and real expertise. Eastman wanted to make it simple for everyone. In 1888 he launched a small camera with a roll of film inside, and a slogan that became legendary: you press the button, we do the rest. You took your pictures, sent the whole camera back, and Kodak developed your photos.

That idea turned photography from a hobby for experts into something for every family on Earth. Birthdays, weddings, holidays, first steps. For almost a hundred years, when people wanted to remember a moment, they used Kodak film. The company became so famous that people started calling special moments Kodak moments. That is how big this brand was. It was not a company, it was part of daily life.

And here is the secret behind the empire. Kodak's cameras were often cheap. The real money came from what you needed after buying one: film, chemicals, paper and processing. Every time you took a picture, Kodak got paid. It is the same model as razors and razor blades, or printers and ink. In the 1970s, Kodak sold around 90 percent of all the film in the United States. The profit margins were enormous. It was one of the most profitable businesses in America.

Now go back to that young engineer, Steve Sasson. His prototype was primitive. The image was just one hundred by one hundred pixels, which is 0.01 megapixels. To see the photo, you had to plug the tape into a special machine connected to a TV. But Sasson and his team understood what this meant. One day, photos would not need film. And if photos did not need film, then Kodak's entire business model would disappear.

The executives understood it too, and that was the problem. Why would a company that makes a fortune from every roll of film promote a technology that needs no film at all? So Kodak did something that looks crazy today but made sense at the time. It kept researching digital, it even registered important patents on it, but it protected film first. Digital was treated as a threat to manage, not as the future to build.

For a while, it looked like a smart decision. In the 1980s and 1990s, film was still king. Kodak had well over 100,000 employees, reaching roughly 145,000 at its peak. Its revenues in the mid nineties were around 16 billion dollars a year. Wall Street loved it. Why change a machine that was printing money? If you enjoy these stories about giants that fell, subscribe, because this channel is all about the mistakes that cost billions.

But digital technology improves every year, and it does not care about anyone's business model. By the early 2000s, digital cameras were getting cheaper and better. And here is a twist most people do not know: Kodak actually became one of the biggest sellers of digital cameras in the United States. It was number one for a moment in the mid 2000s. So it did react. The problem was that it lost money on many of those cameras.

Selling a digital camera is a one time sale. There is no film, no chemicals, no processing. The old machine that made money every time you pressed the button was gone. And then something even worse happened. In 2007, the iPhone arrived. Within a few years, the camera in everybody's pocket became good enough for most people. Nobody needed to buy a separate camera at all, digital or not.

But this is the part that hurts the most. In 2001, Kodak bought a photo sharing website called Ofoto. People could upload their pictures and share them online. Does that sound familiar? Kodak owned a photo sharing platform before Facebook and years before Instagram. But Kodak used it mainly to get people to order printed photos. In other words, it used the future to try to sell the past.

In 2012, two very different things happened. Facebook bought Instagram, a photo sharing app with only 13 employees, for 1 billion dollars. And Kodak, which once had around 145,000 employees, filed for bankruptcy protection. That same year, Kodak sold Ofoto, by then called Kodak Gallery, to Shutterfly for roughly 24 million dollars. The idea was the same. The mindset was completely different.

The bankruptcy was brutal. Kodak stopped making cameras. It sold many of its digital imaging patents for around 525 million dollars to a group of tech companies. Tens of thousands of jobs had already disappeared over the years, and the city of Rochester, New York, which had grown around Kodak, felt the pain for decades. The company survived, but as a much smaller business focused on printing and chemicals.

And to see that this was not inevitable, look at Kodak's biggest rival: Fujifilm, from Japan. Fujifilm faced exactly the same problem. Its film business was collapsing too. But Fujifilm asked a different question: what else can we do with everything we know about chemistry and film? It moved into medical imaging, into special materials for screens, and even into skincare cosmetics, using the same knowledge it had used to stop photos from fading. It was painful, and it cut thousands of jobs. But Fujifilm survived as a big company. Same storm, different decision.

So was Kodak run by stupid people? No. And that is the scary lesson. Kodak's leaders were smart, and their decisions made sense year after year. Every single year, protecting film was the most profitable choice. The problem is that a series of smart short term decisions can add up to one catastrophic long term mistake. Business experts call this the innovator's dilemma.

The companies that survive disruption are the ones willing to destroy their own business before someone else does. Apple did it when the iPhone killed the iPod. Netflix did it when streaming killed its DVD business. Kodak could have done it in 1975, with a prototype in its own laboratory, years before any competitor. Instead, it waited, and the future arrived anyway.

Today, people take more photos in a single day than they used to take in years. Photography did not die. It exploded. The irony is that the company that made photography popular for everyone missed the biggest photography boom in history. And Steve Sasson, the young engineer with the toaster sized camera, was later honored at the White House for his invention.

So here is my question for you. Can you think of a company today that is making the same mistake Kodak made, protecting an old business while the future is already here? Tell me in the comments, and let's see if we can predict the next Kodak.

segments.text: In 1975, a Kodak engineer invented the first digital camera. It weighed around 8 pounds and took 23 seconds to save one photo. His bosses said: that's cute, but don't tell anyone. Why? Because Kodak made a fortune selling film, and digital cameras need no film. So Kodak waited. In 2012, the same year Instagram sold for 1 billion dollars, Kodak filed for bankruptcy, killed by its own invention. The full story is on the channel.
